title: What If Earth Stopped Spinning Because of You?

beats.text: solen står kvar kl 21, dagen blir 30 timmar
kronan sitter fast, +4 min i timmen (slutlöfte)
Vole: $2 miljoner för att låta det vara
Priyas regel: en sekund i taget (planterad)
kronan har fastnat – klockan går bakåt själv
kugghjulet vill slå tillbaka i ett hopp
valet: ett hopp eller ett klick i taget

scenes.say: It's 9 p.m. in Denver, the sun is still up, and today will last 30 hours.
Thousands of people on 16th Street are filming a sunset that never came.
This is every level of slowing the planet, and the real science behind each one.
Your watch is stuck. The day keeps stretching, 4 more minutes every hour.

fact_strip.head: THAT'S REAL
fact_strip.text: Earth makes one full turn every 23 hours, 56 minutes and 4.09 seconds
fact_strip.source: Live Science, 'What would happen if Earth stopped spinning?' (2021)

scenes.say: Grant Vole is offering you 2 million dollars to leave the planet exactly like this.
The ground at the equator moves about 1,037 miles per hour. In New York City, about 794.

visual.head: THAT'S REAL
visual.text: Earth's spin at the equator (794 mph in New York City)
visual.source: Astronomy magazine, 'What happens if Earth stops rotating?' (Feb 2026)

scenes.say: And across town, an 82-year-old man named Abe is on his knees beside a pendulum, drawing chalk lines on the floor.

fact_strip.head: THAT'S REAL
fact_strip.text: Léon Foucault first showed Earth turning with a pendulum on February 3, 1851, in Paris
fact_strip.source: APS News, 'February 3, 1851: Léon Foucault Demonstrates That Earth Rotates'

scenes.say: So, what if Earth stopped spinning because of you?

visual.text: the planet's brake is on your wrist

scenes.say: Day 1 is a short gray afternoon in November, 31 stories up the side of a glass tower in downtown Denver.
Level one is a single millisecond, and it's so small that nobody on Earth can feel it.

visual.text: ONE MILLISECOND: nobody notices

scenes.say: You wash windows for a living, and you get paid by the pane, so every minute of daylight is money in your pocket.

fact_strip.head: THAT'S REAL
fact_strip.text: NASA: the 2004 Sumatra earthquake shifted the mean North Pole about 1 inch
fact_strip.source: NASA JPL, 'NASA Details Earthquake Effects on the Earth' (2005)

scenes.say: Rosa Delgado runs the crew. Every afternoon she taps her hard hat at the sky and says the same four words. The sun's the boss.
At lunch you find an old brass wristwatch in a planter box on the 31st floor, and nobody in the building has ever seen it.

fact_strip.head: THAT'S REAL
fact_strip.text: Earth's spin energy was gained as the planet formed 4.6 billion years ago
fact_strip.source: Scientific American, 'If I stop the world, will I melt with you?'

scenes.say: Out of habit, you wind the crown backward one click. The second hand stutters, and for a moment the whole city seems to sigh.
A normal day is already a little longer than 24 hours. On average, it runs about two thousandths of a second over.

visual.head: THAT'S REAL
visual.text: an average day, compared with exactly 24 hours
visual.source: timeanddate.com, 'Leap seconds' (Dr. Bruce Warrington)

scenes.say: Nothing looks different. Rosa is still yelling about streaks on the 30th floor, and the sun goes down right on schedule.

fact_strip.head: THAT'S REAL
fact_strip.text: The extra bit adds up to one whole second in about 1.5 years
fact_strip.source: timeanddate.com, 'Leap seconds'

scenes.say: Earth's speed really does wobble. The shortest day ever recorded was June 29, 2022, at 1.59 milliseconds under 24 hours.

visual.head: THAT'S REAL
visual.text: the shortest day on record: 1.59 ms under 24 hours
visual.source: Wikipedia, 'Leap second'

scenes.say: Big events nudge it too. NASA calculated that the 2004 Sumatra earthquake shortened every day by 2.68 microseconds.

visual.head: THAT'S REAL
visual.text: shorter days after the 2004 Sumatra earthquake
visual.source: NASA JPL, 'NASA Details Earthquake Effects on the Earth' (2005)

scenes.say: NASA compared it to a spinning skater pulling her arms closer to her body. Move mass toward the middle, and the spin speeds up.

visual.head: THAT'S REAL
visual.text: pull the mass in, spin faster
visual.source: NASA JPL, 'NASA Details Earthquake Effects on the Earth' (2005)

scenes.say: That night you test it at your kitchen table. One click backward, and an atomic clock app on your phone shows the day stretch a hair.
Even a dam could do it. NASA worked out that filling China's Three Gorges reservoir would make the day 0.06 microseconds longer.

visual.head: THAT'S REAL
visual.text: the Three Gorges reservoir, filled (40 cubic km of water)
visual.source: NASA JPL, 'NASA Details Earthquake Effects on the Earth' (2005)

scenes.say: Level one verdict: one click makes the day a millisecond longer, and not one person on the planet notices a thing.

fact_strip.head: THAT'S REAL
fact_strip.text: A filled Three Gorges reservoir would also shift the pole about 0.8 inch
fact_strip.source: NASA JPL, 'NASA Details Earthquake Effects on the Earth' (2005)

scenes.say: Day 3, and you get a little greedy. You give the crown a thousand clicks backward before your morning coffee.
Level two is one extra second, and it turns out that the world's computers really hate surprises.

visual.text: ONE SECOND: 86,401

scenes.say: A day with a leap second really has 86,401 seconds in it, instead of the usual 86,400.

visual.head: THAT'S REAL
visual.text: seconds in a day with a leap second
visual.source: timeanddate.com, 'Leap seconds'

scenes.say: Your neighbor Priya Shah runs the night computers at a hospital downtown, and at midnight her phone starts ringing nonstop.
Every clock in her building now disagrees with every other clock, and the medicine carts are waiting on screens that freeze.
The first real leap second was added on June 30, 1972. There have been 27 so far, and the last was December 31, 2016.

visual.head: THAT'S REAL
visual.text: June 30, 1972 to December 31, 2016
visual.source: NIST, 'Leap Seconds'; Wikipedia, 'Leap second'

scenes.say: They exist to keep atomic clock time within 0.9 seconds of the time set by the Earth's actual spin.

visual.head: THAT'S REAL
visual.text: how close UTC is kept to Earth's spin (UT1)
visual.source: NIST, 'Leap Seconds'

scenes.say: Extra seconds have caused real trouble. After the June 2012 leap second, Qantas, Mozilla and many Linux sites reported problems.

visual.head: THAT'S REAL
visual.text: Qantas, Mozilla and Linux sites hit by flawed software
visual.source: Wikipedia, 'Leap second'

scenes.say: By 3 a.m. Priya has it fixed. She tapes a note above her desk that just says 86,401, and draws an angry face next to it.
Over coffee in the hallway you tell her the truth. She thinks you're joking, but she still gives you one rule.

fact_strip.head: THAT'S REAL
fact_strip.text: In 2015, Netflix, Amazon and Apple's Beats 1 also had interruptions around a leap second
fact_strip.source: Wikipedia, 'Leap second'

scenes.say: If you ever touch a clock again, change it one second at a time, slowly, and never all in one big jump.
The world's timekeepers have had enough too. In 2022 they voted to drop leap seconds in or before 2035.

visual.head: THAT'S REAL
visual.text: leap seconds to be dropped (CGPM, 2022)
visual.source: Wikipedia, 'Leap second'

scenes.say: Level two verdict: one second is too small to feel, but big enough to make an entire hospital panic for three hours.

fact_strip.head: THAT'S REAL
fact_strip.text: UTC currently runs 37 seconds behind atomic time (TAI)
fact_strip.source: NIST, 'Leap Seconds'

scenes.say: Day 6, at the science museum, where your crew is washing the big glass dome over the main hall.
Level three is one whole minute, and a very old man with a box of chalk.

visual.text: ONE MINUTE: Abe notices

scenes.say: In the middle of the hall, a heavy brass ball swings on a long wire above a ring of little wooden pegs.

fact_strip.head: THAT'S REAL
fact_strip.text: In 1851 Foucault also hung a 28 kg ball inside the dome of the Panthéon in Paris
fact_strip.source: Britannica, 'Foucault pendulum'

scenes.say: Abe Lindqvist has volunteered here for 31 years. Every hour, he marks on the floor which peg the pendulum just knocked over.
That's a real experiment. In 1851, Léon Foucault hung a 28 kilogram brass bob on a 67 meter wire to show the Earth turning.

visual.head: THAT'S REAL
visual.text: a 28 kg bob on a 67 m wire, Paris
visual.source: APS News, 'February 3, 1851: Léon Foucault Demonstrates That Earth Rotates'

scenes.say: The swing keeps its direction while the floor turns underneath it. In Paris, that swing turns about 270 degrees in a day.

visual.head: THAT'S REAL
visual.text: how far Foucault's pendulum turns in a day in Paris
visual.source: APS News, 'February 3, 1851: Léon Foucault Demonstrates That Earth Rotates'

scenes.say: At the North Pole it would turn a full circle in 24 hours. At the equator, it wouldn't turn at all.

visual.head: THAT'S REAL
visual.text: at the North Pole. At the equator: never.
visual.source: APS News, 'February 3, 1851: Léon Foucault Demonstrates That Earth Rotates'

scenes.say: That morning, hanging from the dome, you click the crown back sixty thousand times, and the day gets one minute longer.
Down below, Abe stares at his chalk marks. The pegs are falling late. He checks his pocket watch twice, then looks straight up at you.

fact_strip.head: THAT'S REAL
fact_strip.text: At the equator the ground moves about 1,000 to 1,100 mph, depending on the source
fact_strip.source: Space.com (2024); Live Science (2021)

scenes.say: He doesn't say a word. He writes LATE on the floor in chalk, underlines it twice, and keeps on watching you.
At lunch he sits next to you on the museum steps and says the floor doesn't lie. Something slowed down, and it was you.

fact_strip.head: THAT'S REAL
fact_strip.text: At the poles, the ground's spinning speed drops to zero
fact_strip.source: Astronomy magazine, 'What happens if Earth stops rotating?' (Feb 2026)

scenes.say: Then Abe makes you a deal. He'll keep chalk marks every hour, and you'll tell him every time you touch that watch.
Level three verdict: one minute is the first change a careful person can measure, and Abe is the most careful person you know.

fact_strip.head: THAT'S REAL
fact_strip.text: In 100 years, each day is predicted to be about 0.004 seconds longer on average
fact_strip.source: timeanddate.com, 'Leap seconds'

scenes.say: Day 10, and you finally do the thing you wanted on day 1. You turn the crown back a full hour.
Level four is one whole hour, and a day that lasts 25 of them.

visual.text: 25 HOURS: more daylight

scenes.say: The afternoon stretches out like taffy, and you squeeze in another 40 windows before it gets dark.

fact_strip.head: THAT'S REAL
fact_strip.text: The rudist clam lived for over nine years in a shallow tropical seabed
fact_strip.source: AGU, 'Ancient shell shows days were half-hour shorter 70 million years ago' (2020)

scenes.say: Rosa does the math on a napkin. At three dollars a pane, the crew makes 120 dollars more every day, and she's thrilled.
Earth really did spin faster once. 70 million years ago, a day lasted only about 23 and a half hours.

visual.head: THAT'S REAL
visual.text: the length of a day 70 million years ago
visual.source: AGU, 'Ancient shell shows days were half-hour shorter 70 million years ago' (2020)

scenes.say: Scientists got that from a fossil rudist clam that lived more than nine years and grew a thin layer every single day.

visual.head: THAT'S REAL
visual.text: a fossil rudist clam, 9+ years of growth
visual.source: AGU, 'Ancient shell shows days were half-hour shorter 70 million years ago' (2020)

scenes.say: Counting those layers gave 372 days in a year back then, compared with our 365.

visual.head: THAT'S REAL
visual.text: in a year, 70 million years ago
visual.source: AGU, 'Ancient shell shows days were half-hour shorter 70 million years ago' (2020)

scenes.say: The Moon is the brake. It drifts away from Earth by about 3.82 centimeters, or one and a half inches, every year.

visual.head: THAT'S REAL
visual.text: how far the Moon moves away each year
visual.source: AGU, 'Ancient shell shows days were half-hour shorter 70 million years ago' (2020)

scenes.say: Tidal friction from the Moon alone would lengthen the day by about 2.3 milliseconds every century.

visual.head: THAT'S REAL
visual.text: per century, from tidal friction alone
visual.source: Wikipedia, 'Leap second'

scenes.say: Then the news picks it up. Atomic clocks all over the world are drifting, and the experts on TV don't have a good answer.

fact_strip.head: THAT'S REAL
fact_strip.text: The length of a day has been increasing by about 1.4 to 1.7 ms per century
fact_strip.source: Wikipedia, 'Leap second'

scenes.say: The next morning Grant Vole calls. He owns Vole Freight, all 9,000 trucks, and he saw a museum photo of you on the dome.
His offer is simple. Keep the day at 25 hours forever, and he'll pay you a million dollars a year to do it.
His trucks would get an extra hour every day, and so would his drivers, whether they wanted one or not.

fact_strip.head: THAT'S REAL
fact_strip.text: The day has gotten longer because of tidal forces from the Moon
fact_strip.source: xkcd What If?, 'Leap Seconds' (Randall Munroe)

scenes.say: A million dollars a year. You've never even seen one hundred thousand in one place.
Level four verdict: one extra hour feels like a gift, and somebody already wants to buy it from you.

fact_strip.head: THAT'S REAL
fact_strip.text: Half a billion years ago, each day was about 22 hours long
fact_strip.source: xkcd What If?, 'Leap Seconds' (Randall Munroe)

scenes.say: Day 18. Vole sends a bonus check anyway, and you click the crown back two more hours, just to see what happens.
Level five is a 27-hour day, and the sky starts acting strange.

visual.text: 27 HOURS: the wind changes

scenes.say: Up on the tower, the wind keeps coming from directions Rosa has never seen, so she ties every line on the platform twice.

fact_strip.head: THAT'S REAL
fact_strip.text: Hurricanes and typhoons are low-pressure systems
fact_strip.source: NOAA NESDIS, 'What is the Coriolis Effect?'

scenes.say: Earth's spin shapes the weather. Air and ocean currents are strongly influenced by the planet's rotation.

visual.head: THAT'S REAL
visual.text: air and ocean currents follow Earth's rotation
visual.source: Space.com, 'What would happen if Earth stopped spinning?' (2024)

scenes.say: The spin is also why big storms twist. They spin counterclockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and clockwise in the Southern.

visual.head: THAT'S REAL
visual.text: storms: counterclockwise north, clockwise south
visual.source: NOAA SciJinks, 'A Powerful Force'

scenes.say: The reason is that different parts of the Earth move at different speeds, which bends the air flowing into a storm.

visual.head: THAT'S REAL
visual.text: that deflection is what makes cyclones spin
visual.source: NOAA NESDIS, 'What is the Coriolis Effect?'

scenes.say: The slow, gentle change in this story is made up. Everything on a card like this one is real.

visual.text: the watch is fiction. the cards are real.

scenes.say: Abe calls you to the museum at closing time. His hourly chalk marks have turned into a long, crooked line across the floor.

fact_strip.head: THAT'S REAL
fact_strip.text: If Earth stopped, the poles would likely be the least affected places
fact_strip.source: Space.com, 'What would happen if Earth stopped spinning?' (2024)

scenes.say: He points at the pegs and says, every hour you add, my pendulum gets lazier. And after the pendulum, it's the oceans.
Earth is fatter at the equator than at the poles. NOAA says that bulge comes from the force of the planet's constant spin.

visual.head: THAT'S REAL
visual.text: Earth's spin makes it bulge at the equator
visual.source: NOAA Ocean Service, 'Is the Earth round?'

scenes.say: If the spin stopped, that would fade, and Astronomy magazine says ocean water would migrate rapidly toward the poles.

visual.head: THAT'S REAL
visual.text: toward the poles, if Earth stopped spinning
visual.source: Astronomy magazine, 'What happens if Earth stops rotating?' (Feb 2026)

scenes.say: Priya shows you the hospital logs. Every system she runs now has to be corrected by hand, three times a day.

fact_strip.head: THAT'S REAL
fact_strip.text: Earth's magnetic field is linked to flowing liquid metal in the outer core
fact_strip.source: Space.com, 'What would happen if Earth stopped spinning?' (2024)

scenes.say: Level five verdict: every hour you add makes the sky, the sea and every clock on Earth work harder to keep up with you.

fact_strip.head: THAT'S REAL
fact_strip.text: Earth's magnetic field protects us from harmful radiation from space
fact_strip.source: Space.com, 'What would happen if Earth stopped spinning?' (2024)

scenes.say: Day 24, and Vole wants more. He sends a black car to bring you up to his office on the 50th floor.
Level six is Grant Vole, a man who thinks a planet is just a very big truck.

visual.text: GRANT VOLE: wants it to stop

scenes.say: He wants a 30-hour day, and he has done the math. Every extra hour means more deliveries out of every driver.

fact_strip.head: THAT'S REAL
fact_strip.text: A sudden stop would likely trigger tsunamis and earthquakes
fact_strip.source: Space.com, 'What would happen if Earth stopped spinning?' (2024)

scenes.say: Then he leans in and asks what happens if you just stop it, because a day that never ends could be very good for business.
Scientists have worked that out. If Earth stopped suddenly, the equator would get winds of more than 1,000 miles per hour.

visual.head: THAT'S REAL
visual.text: winds at the equator after a sudden stop
visual.source: Astronomy magazine, 'What happens if Earth stops rotating?' (Feb 2026)

scenes.say: The air, water and buildings would all keep moving at their old speed, and almost all structures would collapse at once.

visual.head: THAT'S REAL
visual.text: almost all structures would collapse at once
visual.source: Astronomy magazine, 'What happens if Earth stops rotating?' (Feb 2026)

scenes.say: If it slowed down gradually instead, days and nights would keep stretching until each one lasted six months.

visual.head: THAT'S REAL
visual.text: of day, then 6 months of night
visual.source: Space.com, 'What would happen if Earth stopped spinning?' (2024)

scenes.say: Stopping Earth would take a lot of energy. Scientific American puts its spin energy at about 200 octillion joules.

visual.head: THAT'S REAL
visual.text: the energy stored in Earth's spin
visual.source: Scientific American, 'If I stop the world, will I melt with you?'

scenes.say: That's roughly a million times the energy of the asteroid that hit Earth 66 million years ago.

visual.head: THAT'S REAL
visual.text: the dinosaur-killing asteroid's energy
visual.source: Scientific American, 'If I stop the world, will I melt with you?'

scenes.say: You say no and walk out. In the elevator, you try to click the crown forward, back toward 24 hours.

fact_strip.head: THAT'S REAL
fact_strip.text: A Falcon 9 rocket can generate about a trillion joules of energy
fact_strip.source: Scientific American, 'If I stop the world, will I melt with you?'

scenes.say: It won't move. The crown is jammed tight, and the second hand is creeping backward all on its own.
Abe works it out from his chalk marks. The day is getting about a minute longer every hour, and the rate keeps climbing.
Level six verdict: a sudden stop would wreck the planet, and now the watch is slowing it down without you.

fact_strip.head: THAT'S REAL
fact_strip.text: There is no natural force that would stop the Earth from spinning
fact_strip.source: Live Science (2021)

scenes.say: Day 30, 9 p.m., and the sun still hasn't set over 16th Street.
Level seven is the moment you saw at the very start of this video, and the watch is still turning backward.

visual.text: 30 HOURS: and growing

scenes.say: Down on the street, thousands of people are filming the sky. Up on your tower, Rosa holds the platform steady in the wind.

fact_strip.head: THAT'S REAL
fact_strip.text: Earth will never actually stop rotating
fact_strip.source: Astronomy magazine, 'What happens if Earth stops rotating?' (Feb 2026)

scenes.say: Vole calls again. Two million dollars to stop at 30 hours. You hang up, because this was never his day to sell.
You could smash the watch, but you have no idea what one sudden jump would do to a planet that has been slowing for a month.

fact_strip.head: THAT'S REAL
fact_strip.text: A sudden stop: winds of more than 1,000 mph at the equator
fact_strip.source: Astronomy magazine, 'What happens if Earth stops rotating?' (Feb 2026)

scenes.say: Then you remember the note above Priya's desk. 86,401. Change it one second at a time, and never in one big jump.
You call her, and she drives to the museum with a laptop and a tiny screwdriver from the hospital's repair kit.
Abe is already there, on his knees beside the pendulum, with a fresh box of chalk and his old pocket watch.

fact_strip.head: THAT'S REAL
fact_strip.text: In 1851, Foucault's pendulum showed the Earth turning, in Paris
fact_strip.source: APS News, 'February 3, 1851: Léon Foucault Demonstrates That Earth Rotates'

scenes.say: Priya opens the back of the watch. The crown isn't broken at all. A single grain of grit is wedged against one gear.
She can pull it out, but then the gear will snap forward to 24 hours all at once, unless someone holds it back by hand.

fact_strip.head: THAT'S REAL
fact_strip.text: The 28th CGPM, set for 2026, is expected to review the new leap-second limit
fact_strip.source: Wikipedia, 'Leap second'

scenes.say: So that's the choice. Let the gear snap back in one jump, or hold it and let it creep forward one click at a time, all night.

visual.title: THE CHOICE
lines: A: one jump back to 24 hours
B: one click at a time, all night

scenes.say: You hold the crown with your thumbnail. Priya pulls the grit free. The gear shoves hard against your thumb, and you don't let go.

fact_strip.head: THAT'S REAL
fact_strip.text: Russia asked to push the end of leap seconds back to 2040
fact_strip.source: Wikipedia, 'Leap second'

scenes.say: One click. Abe calls out the chalk mark. One more click, and he calls it again. You keep that rhythm for nine hours.
Earth's spin has been speeding up lately. In 2020 the planet had the 28 shortest days measured since 1960.

visual.head: THAT'S REAL
visual.text: in 2020, the most since 1960
visual.source: Wikipedia, 'Leap second'

scenes.say: That speed-up is why Astronomy magazine says a leap second might even have to be subtracted, possibly in 2029.

visual.head: THAT'S REAL
visual.text: a negative leap second has never happened
visual.source: Astronomy magazine, 'What happens if Earth stops rotating?' (Feb 2026)

scenes.say: Around 4 a.m. the pegs start falling on time again. Abe stops writing LATE. He writes OK, and then he writes it again.
At sunrise Priya checks the hospital clocks. 86,400 seconds. A normal day, give or take a couple of milliseconds.

fact_strip.head: THAT'S REAL
fact_strip.text: An average day runs about 0.002 seconds over 24 hours
fact_strip.source: timeanddate.com, 'Leap seconds'

scenes.say: The sun comes up over the Rocky Mountains right where it should, and down on 16th Street, people finally go to bed.

fact_strip.head: THAT'S REAL
fact_strip.text: NASA: the 2004 quake made Earth about one part in 10 billion less flattened
fact_strip.source: NASA JPL, 'NASA Details Earthquake Effects on the Earth' (2005)

scenes.say: Vole sends one last message. He says you just threw away two million dollars. You send him a photo of the sunrise.
Rosa taps her hard hat at the sky, exactly the way she did on day 1, and says it again. The sun's the boss.

fact_strip.head: THAT'S REAL
fact_strip.text: It takes about a decade for Earth's core to sync up with its crust
fact_strip.source: xkcd What If?, 'Leap Seconds' (Randall Munroe)

scenes.say: You give the watch to Abe. He locks it in the glass case next to the pendulum, with a little card that says do not wind.
Rosa, Priya, Abe, Grant Vole and the watch are made up. The spinning Earth, the clocks and the clam are all real.

visual.text: the people and the watch are fiction. the science is real.

scenes.say: And one more real one. Spinning in an office chair really does change Earth's rotation, just not enough to matter.

visual.head: THAT'S REAL
visual.text: temporarily alters Earth's spin, not enough to matter
visual.source: xkcd What If?, 'Leap Seconds' (Randall Munroe)

scenes.say: Your turn. On day 30, would you let the gear snap back in one jump, or hold it all night, one click at a time? A or B.

visual.title: WHAT WOULD YOU DO?
lines: B: one click at a time

scenes.say: Level 8 is coming next. What if you were the last man on earth, and every clock still kept running?
Until then, watch a sunset tonight. Every one of them is the Earth turning at about a thousand miles an hour, right on time.

fact_strip.head: THAT'S REAL
fact_strip.text: Earth spins at around 1,000 mph at the equator
fact_strip.source: Space.com, 'What would happen if Earth stopped spinning?' (2024)

seo.hook: It's 9 p.m. in Denver, the sun is still up, and today will last 30 hours. Thousands of people on 16th Street are filming a sunset that never came.
seo.summary:
What if Earth started spinning slower, and you were the reason? You wash windows on a glass tower in downtown Denver, and one gray afternoon in November you find an old brass watch in a planter box. Turn the crown backward and the whole planet slows down. Level by level, you add a millisecond, then a second that crashes a hospital's computers, then a minute that an 82-year-old museum volunteer catches with a Foucault pendulum and a piece of chalk, then a whole hour. A freight boss offers you a million dollars a year to keep the 25-hour day. On day 30 the crown is jammed, the sun is still up at 9 p.m., and the day is getting longer every hour.

This is a fictional What If story. The watch and every character (Rosa, Priya, Abe, Grant Vole) are made up. The facts on screen are real:
- The ground at the equator moves about 1,037 mph (794 mph in New York City); a sudden stop would mean winds over 1,000 mph and almost all structures collapsing; ocean water would migrate toward the poles; Earth will never actually stop rotating (Astronomy magazine, 2026)
- A gradual stop would stretch day and night to six months each; air and ocean currents follow Earth's rotation (Space.com, 2024)
- One rotation takes 23 h 56 min 4.09 s; no natural force would stop Earth spinning (Live Science, 2021)
- Earth's spin energy is about 2 × 10^29 joules, about a million times the dinosaur-killing asteroid (Scientific American)
- The 2004 Sumatra earthquake shortened the day by 2.68 microseconds; a filled Three Gorges reservoir would lengthen it by 0.06 microseconds (NASA JPL)
- 27 leap seconds since June 30, 1972, the last on December 31, 2016; UTC is kept within 0.9 s of Earth's spin and is 37 s behind TAI (NIST, Wikipedia)
- The June 2012 leap second caused problems at Qantas, Mozilla and many Linux sites; leap seconds are to be dropped in or before 2035 (Wikipedia)
- The shortest day on record was June 29, 2022, 1.59 ms under 24 hours; an average day runs about 0.002 s over (Wikipedia, timeanddate.com)
- Foucault's 1851 pendulum: 28 kg bob, 67 m wire, about 270° a day in Paris (APS News, Britannica)
- Storms spin counterclockwise in the Northern Hemisphere because different parts of Earth move at different speeds (NOAA)
- 70 million years ago a day was about 23.5 hours and a year had 372 days, from a fossil rudist clam; the Moon recedes 3.82 cm a year (AGU, 2020)
- Earth bulges at the equator because of its spin (NOAA Ocean Service)
- Spinning in an office chair changes Earth's rotation, but not enough to matter (xkcd What If?)
seo.description:
What if Earth started spinning slower, and you were the reason? You wash windows on a glass tower in downtown Denver, and one gray afternoon in November you find an old brass watch in a planter box. Turn the crown backward and the whole planet slows down. Level by level, you add a millisecond, then a second that crashes a hospital's computers, then a minute that an 82-year-old museum volunteer catches with a Foucault pendulum and a piece of chalk, then a whole hour. A freight boss offers you a million dollars a year to keep the 25-hour day. On day 30 the crown is jammed, the sun is still up at 9 p.m., and the day is getting longer every hour.

This is a fictional What If story. The watch and every character (Rosa, Priya, Abe, Grant Vole) are made up. The facts on screen are real:
- The ground at the equator moves about 1,037 mph (794 mph in New York City); a sudden stop would mean winds over 1,000 mph and almost all structures collapsing; ocean water would migrate toward the poles; Earth will never actually stop rotating (Astronomy magazine, 2026)
- A gradual stop would stretch day and night to six months each; air and ocean currents follow Earth's rotation (Space.com, 2024)
- One rotation takes 23 h 56 min 4.09 s; no natural force would stop Earth spinning (Live Science, 2021)
- Earth's spin energy is about 2 × 10^29 joules, about a million times the dinosaur-killing asteroid (Scientific American)
- The 2004 Sumatra earthquake shortened the day by 2.68 microseconds; a filled Three Gorges reservoir would lengthen it by 0.06 microseconds (NASA JPL)
- 27 leap seconds since June 30, 1972, the last on December 31, 2016; UTC is kept within 0.9 s of Earth's spin and is 37 s behind TAI (NIST, Wikipedia)
- The June 2012 leap second caused problems at Qantas, Mozilla and many Linux sites; leap seconds are to be dropped in or before 2035 (Wikipedia)
- The shortest day on record was June 29, 2022, 1.59 ms under 24 hours; an average day runs about 0.002 s over (Wikipedia, timeanddate.com)
- Foucault's 1851 pendulum: 28 kg bob, 67 m wire, about 270° a day in Paris (APS News, Britannica)
- Storms spin counterclockwise in the Northern Hemisphere because different parts of Earth move at different speeds (NOAA)
- 70 million years ago a day was about 23.5 hours and a year had 372 days, from a fossil rudist clam; the Moon recedes 3.82 cm a year (AGU, 2020)
- Earth bulges at the equator because of its spin (NOAA Ocean Service)
- Spinning in an office chair changes Earth's rotation, but not enough to matter (xkcd What If?)
seo.disclaimer: This is a fictional What If story. The watch and all characters are made up; the Earth, time and weather facts are real and sourced below.

standard_check.krok: 0 s hotet (solen uppe kl 21, 30 timmar), 6 s vändningen (solnedgången som aldrig kom), 11 s löftet i klartext ('every level of slowing the planet, and the real science behind each one'), 18 s slutlöfte + klocka (kronan fast, +4 min i timmen), 24 s gåta (Vole $2 M), 30 s första faktakortet (1 037 mph), 37 s gåta (Abe och kritan), 45 s titelfrågan. Ingen presentation före första händelsen.
standard_check.nivåer: LEVEL 1 One millisecond · 2 One second (Priya) · 3 One minute (Abe) · 4 The 25-hour day · 5 The weather · 6 Grant Vole · 7 The longest day · Level 8: ??? (last man on earth). Dom efter varje nivå.
standard_check.verkligt_faktum_per_nivå: 1: dygnslängd +0,002 s, rekorddagen 2022, Sumatra 2,68 µs + skridskoåkaren, Three Gorges 0,06 µs · 2: 86 401, 27 skottsekunder 1972–2016, ±0,9 s, 2012-felen, 2035 · 3: Foucault 1851 (28 kg, 67 m, 270°, polerna) · 4: 23,5 h för 70 Ma, 372 dagar, rudistmusslan, Månen 3,82 cm/år, 2,3 ms/sekel · 5: rotation styr strömmar, Coriolis, ekvatorsvällningen, haven mot polerna · 6: 1 000 mph vindar, kollaps, 6 månaders dag, 2×10^29 J, ×1 000 000 asteroiden · 7: 2020 28 korta dagar, negativ skottsekund 2029? · Slut: kontorsstolen (xkcd).
standard_check.planteringar_som_betalas: 1) Priyas regel 'one second at a time, never one big jump' (nivå 2) → valet i klimax · 2) lappen 86,401 (nivå 2) → 86,400 vid soluppgången · 3) Abes kritmärken varje timme (nivå 3) → han ropar ut varje klick, LATE blir OK · 4) Rosas 'The sun's the boss' (nivå 1) → sista repliken · 5) Volés erbjudande $1 M/år (nivå 4) → $2 M i klimax, du skickar soluppgångsbilden · 6) Sudden stop = 1 000 mph (nivå 6) → därför kan du inte krossa klockan · 7) klockan i blomlådan (nivå 1) → DO NOT WIND i montern.
standard_check.känsloslag: Abe skriver LATE och tittar upp på dig, Priyas arga ansikte på lappen, nio timmar med tummen mot kugghjulet, LATE blir OK.
standard_check.moraliskt_val: Mitt i: Voles miljon per år för att behålla 25-timmarsdygnet. Klimax: ett snabbt hopp tillbaka (risk för planeten) eller en sekund i taget hela natten; och $2 M mot en vanlig dag. Speglar kroken.
standard_check.slut: Fråga A/B till tittaren + fäst kommentar, 'Level 8: ???', ett verkligt fenomen att se i kväll (solnedgången = jorden som snurrar) och fiktionskortet.
standard_check.bilder: Wide första 30 s (0 medium), 5 närbilder (första vid ~6:12), 3 tavlor, 1 ritning, 32 THAT'S REAL-kort, scene-andel 49%. Tystnad (silence) vid klicket dag 1, kronan som fastnar och när du håller emot.

krokvarianter: A (VALD – visuell, fungerar utan ljud, matchar miniatyren): 'It's 9 p.m. in Denver, the sun is still up, and today is going to last 30 hours.' + filmande folkmassa.
B (kraften först): 'Every time you turn this watch backward, the whole planet spins a little slower. Tonight the crown is stuck.'
C (tittaren deltar): 'Look at the time on your screen. Now imagine the sun is still up, and it's going to stay up for another 9 hours.'
